title: Map Projection Explorer
subtitle: Visualize and compare common cartographic map projections, graticules, Tissot indicatrices, and distortion properties with interactive D3.js rendering.

overview.heading: Understanding Map Projections
overview.description: Map projections transform the spherical three-dimensional surface of the Earth onto a two-dimensional planar medium. Carl Friedrich Gauss proved with his Theorema Egregium that a sphere cannot be projected onto a plane without introducing distortion. Consequently, every map projection represents a compromise among preserving area (equivalence), conformal angles and local shapes (orthomorphism), distances from specific origins (equidistance), or navigational directions (loxodromes and great circles).

projections.name: Lambert Azimuthal Equal-Area
projections.description: Preserves area accurately across all regions of the map while projecting directions faithfully from the central point.
projections.pros: Strictly equal-area across global extents; ideal for continental and polar statistical distributions without biasing land masses.
projections.cons: Distorts local shapes and angles progressively as distance from the projection origin increases toward the periphery.
projections.uses: Hemispheric thematic maps, polar research charts, continental demographic atlases, and statistical choropleths.

projections.name: Azimuthal Equidistant
projections.description: Preserves exact distances and true directions from the designated center point to all other locations on the globe.
projections.pros: Accurate linear scale along all radii emanating from the center; straight lines from origin represent shortest geodesic great circles.
projections.cons: Severe angular and areal distortion in outer margins; the point opposite the center is stretched into the entire enclosing boundary circle.
projections.uses: High-frequency radio transmission planning, seismic epicenter distance measurement, strategic polar aviation routing, and the UN emblem.

projections.name: Gnomonic
projections.description: Projects points on the sphere from the Earth's geometric center onto a tangent plane, rendering every great circle as a straight line.
projections.pros: Shortest flight routes and oceanic geodesic paths are always plotted as perfectly straight lines between any two coordinates.
projections.cons: Cannot display a full hemisphere; extreme areal and linear stretching occurs outward from the tangent center.
projections.uses: Aviation flight planning, maritime great-circle navigation plotting, seismic P/S-wave directional analysis, and astrometry.

projections.name: Orthographic
projections.description: Simulates a perspective view of the 3D rotating globe viewed from infinite space, preserving the visual curvature of the horizon.
projections.pros: Intuitive, photorealistic aesthetic resembling views from orbit; excellent for single-hemisphere regional overviews.
projections.cons: Displays only one hemisphere at a time; severe compression and foreshortening near the planetary limb.
projections.uses: Educational graphics, interactive globe widgets, regional contextual insets, space sciences, and editorial media.

projections.name: Stereographic
projections.description: A perspective conformal projection where points are projected from the antipode onto a tangent plane, mapping all circles on the sphere to circles.
projections.pros: Preserves infinitesimal angles, shapes, and mutual bearings around any point; transforms spherical circles into planar circles.
projections.cons: Areal scale expands exponentially away from the center point, creating massive exaggeration in peripheral territories.
projections.uses: Polar navigation charts, structural geology, crystallographic stereonets, deep-sky astronomy star charts, and geophysical fault plane analysis.

projections.name: Albers Equal-Area Conic
projections.description: An equal-area conic projection that minimizes distortion along two selected standard parallels across mid-latitude continental extents.
projections.pros: Preserves relative area flawlessly; balances scale variations evenly between standard parallels with minimal shear distortion.
projections.cons: Neither conformal nor equidistant; polar and equatorial extremes suffer considerable curvature deformation.
projections.uses: Official USGS national atlas maps, US Census Bureau demographic maps, and mid-latitude regional administrative surveys.

projections.name: Lambert Conformal Conic
projections.description: A conformal conic projection conceived by Johann Heinrich Lambert that retains true local shapes and angles along mid-latitude belts.
projections.pros: Preserves angles and shapes locally; straight lines closely approximate great circles over medium continental spans.
projections.cons: Exaggerates surface areas significantly north and south of its designated standard parallels.
projections.uses: ICAO aeronautical sectional charts, national meteorological surface analyses, state plane coordinate systems (SPCS), and air traffic control.

projections.name: Conic Equal-Area
projections.description: General conic equal-area projection configuration designed to maintain uniform surface proportions across temperate regions.
projections.pros: Guarantees that regions of equal geographic area on the spheroid occupy identical pixel extents on the cartographic canvas.
projections.cons: Shape distortion increases non-linearly when moving beyond the standard parallels towards the equator or poles.
projections.uses: Agricultural land-use evaluations, mid-latitude regional vegetation cover atlases, and environmental basin assessments.

projections.name: Conic Equidistant
projections.description: A conic projection that maintains a constant scale along every meridian and along two chosen standard parallels.
projections.pros: Balanced compromise with true linear distances along meridians; simple calculation and clean aesthetic layout.
projections.cons: Neither conformal nor equal-area; introduces moderate distortion across both angles and land parcel sizes.
projections.uses: School reference atlases, transcontinental highway network charts, and mid-latitude country regional profiles.

projections.name: Equirectangular (Plate Carrée)
projections.description: A simple cylindrical projection mapping longitude directly to x and latitude directly to y as an orthogonal Cartesian grid.
projections.pros: Direct 1:1 mapping between Geographic WGS84 coordinate space (lon/lat) and raster pixel matrices; universally intuitive indexing.
projections.cons: Massive shape and areal deformation away from the equator; poles are stretched into horizontal lines as wide as the equator.
projections.uses: GIS raster digital elevation models, global satellite texture wraps, texture coordinates in 3D planetary rendering, and quick spatial previews.

projections.name: Mercator
projections.description: A conformal cylindrical projection formulated by Gerardus Mercator in 1569 that renders lines of constant compass course as straight tracks.
projections.pros: Preserves angles and shapes locally; any straight line is a loxodrome (rhumb line), enabling straightforward marine compass navigation.
projections.cons: Infamous polar area inflation: Greenland appears roughly equal in size to Africa, despite Africa being 14 times larger in reality.
projections.uses: Marine navigational charts, Web Mercator (EPSG:3857) web tiling (OpenStreetMap, Google Maps, Mapbox), and nautical piloting.

projections.name: Transverse Mercator
projections.description: A transverse cylinder orientation rotated 90 degrees relative to standard Mercator, tangent or secant along a specific central meridian.
projections.pros: Highly accurate and minimally distorted within a narrow zone (up to 6 degrees of longitude) surrounding the central meridian.
projections.cons: Scale factor and area error escalate rapidly as one moves east or west away from the standard longitudinal meridian.
projections.uses: Universal Transverse Mercator (UTM) worldwide grid, national cadastral surveys, ordnance mapping, and military topographic charts.
